title: Where State Lives
subtitle: Place durable and ephemeral data according to access and failure requirements
objectives: Identify what counts as state, and why stateless components are trivial to scale
Map the places state can live and the speed/durability/trust tradeoff of each
Distinguish a source of truth from a derived copy, and know why every copy costs consistency
Decide where a given piece of state belongs, using what's lost and who must read it

exercises.title: State is information retained across requests or process restarts
exercises.body: A stateful component keeps information that later operations depend on. A stateless app instance may read shared databases, but no later request depends on request-specific data retained only by that instance. Any equivalent instance can therefore handle the next request.
exercises.note: Request-local memory is compatible with stateless operation. State appears when a later request depends on data kept by a particular process or machine.

exercises.prompt: A user's cart exists only in Server A's memory. Move it to a shared durable store so either server can handle the next request.
exercises.actionLabel: Move the cart to shared storage
exercises.beforeStatus: FAILOVER TEST · Server A stops; the cart disappears
exercises.afterStatus: FAILOVER TEST · Server B reads the same cart from shared storage
exercises.why: Shared durable storage lets any application server retrieve the cart. Moving state out of one server removes that server as the only copy; the shared store now needs its own availability and durability design.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the system for this case: A user's cart exists only in Server A's memory. Move it to a shared durable store so either server can handle the next request. Place Server A, Server B, Cart store. Then connect the components in the direction that requests, data, or events move.
exercises.why: The completed diagram contains these directed flows: User → Server B; Server A → Cart store; Server B → Cart store. That topology is the evidence for the answer: Shared durable storage lets any application server retrieve the cart. Moving state out of one server removes that server as the only copy; the shared store now needs its own availability and durability design.

exercises.prompt: You have two services: one resizes images (input in, output out, remembers nothing) and one stores user profiles. Which is trivially easy to run as 100 copies?
choices: The profile store
The image resizer — it remembers nothing, so any copy can do any job
Both are equally easy
Neither can be copied
exercises.why: The image resizer is stateless because its output depends only on the current input. Any replica can process any image without coordinating stored user data, while profile-store replicas require durability and agreement about updates.

exercises.prompt: A component is ______ if it keeps no memory between requests — so any copy can handle any request.
choices: stateless
idempotent
cached
sharded
exercises.why: A stateless component retains no required request state between calls. Its replicas are interchangeable because the next request carries its inputs or reads shared state elsewhere.

exercises.prompt: Which of these are STATE (something the system must remember)? Select all.
choices: A user's shopping cart
A function that adds two numbers
An uploaded profile photo
The number of likes on a post
exercises.why: Shopping carts, uploaded photos, and like counts must persist information from earlier events, so they are state. A pure addition function retains nothing after returning its result and can recompute the same output from the same inputs.

exercises.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.

pairs.right: Any copy can serve any request
Retains information that affects later operations
The authority used to resolve disagreement
Can be rebuilt from the truth

exercises.why: A stateless component retains no private request history needed by the next operation; a stateful component does retain such information. If state is copied, the design then needs explicit consistency rules, but having multiple copies is not part of the definition of stateful. A source of truth resolves disagreement, while a derived copy can be rebuilt from that authority.

exercises.prompt: Why do horizontally scaled app servers usually keep durable shared state in a database or shared store?
choices: It makes every request stay on one app server
It keeps app servers interchangeable while specialized stores coordinate persistence and shared access
State should be avoided entirely
Move all data to the client
exercises.why: When durable shared state lives in a database or shared store, any app server can load it and handle the next request. The compute tier stays replaceable, while components designed for persistence and coordination enforce the required durability and consistency.

exercises.prompt: Why is a stateless app tier so much easier to operate than a stateful one?
choices: It uses less memory
Any instance can be added, killed, restarted, or replaced at any time with no coordination and nothing lost
It doesn't need a network
It's written in a different language
exercises.why: A stateless instance holds no unique required data, so replacement, autoscaling, and rolling deployment do not require state transfer or user affinity. A stateful instance needs preservation, replication, or recovery before it can disappear safely.

exercises.title: State placement determines durability, visibility, latency, and trust
exercises.body: Client storage, process memory, a shared in-memory store, and a disk-backed database provide different guarantees. Evaluate a value by whether it must survive restarts, which instances must read it, acceptable access latency, and whether the writer is trusted.
exercises.note: Treat client-provided values as untrusted. Authenticate the caller, authorize the action, validate the input, and obtain price, inventory, and permissions from server-controlled truth.

exercises.prompt: A login session exists only in Server A's memory. The next request lands on Server B and appears logged out. Move the session where both servers can read it.
choices: Enable sticky sessions
Add two more stateless servers
Move sessions to a shared store
choiceFeedback: Stickiness can hide the problem during normal routing, but losing Server A still loses its in-memory sessions.
More servers create more places where the session is absent.
A shared store makes the session available to every application server.
exercises.beforeStatus: REQUEST ON SERVER B · session missing
exercises.afterStatus: REQUEST ON SERVER B · session loaded · user remains signed in
exercises.result: The session stopped depending on one server's memory
exercises.why: Shared session storage lets any application server load the same session. Signed client tokens are another option when their contents and revocation model fit the security requirements.

exercises.prompt: Complete the system for this case: A login session exists only in Server A's memory. The next request lands on Server B and appears logged out. Move the session where both servers can read it. Place Server B, Session store. Then connect the components in the direction that requests, data, or events move.
exercises.why: The completed diagram contains these directed flows: User → Server B; Server B → Session store. That topology is the evidence for the answer: Shared session storage lets any application server load the same session. Signed client tokens are another option when their contents and revocation model fit the security requirements.

exercises.prompt: You restart every server in your fleet. Which survives?
choices: Data held in server RAM
Data written to a database on disk
Both survive
Neither survives
exercises.why: Server RAM is volatile and loses its contents when the process or machine restarts. A database on durable storage records committed data beyond process lifetime, although surviving a machine or site failure additionally requires replication.

exercises.prompt: Match each place state can live to its defining property.

pairs.right: Controlled by the client; integrity must be verified before trust
Low-latency shared state, commonly treated as disposable
Durable shared records with query and constraint support

exercises.why: Client state travels with the caller but is caller-controlled, server RAM is fast and volatile, a shared cache gives low-latency cross-server access with limited durability, and a database prioritizes durable authoritative storage. Placement follows the required trust, sharing, latency, and survival properties.

exercises.prompt: You store the shopping cart's total price in a cookie on the client. What's the danger?
choices: Cookies are too slow
The client controls it and can edit it — so a user could set their total to $0
Cookies expire too quickly
There's no danger; it saves a database call
exercises.why: The user controls cookie contents and can modify an unsigned total before sending it back. The server must calculate or verify prices from trusted data; a signature can detect tampering but does not make arbitrary client-provided values authoritative.

exercises.prompt: Which are good reasons to put state in a shared cache like Redis instead of the database? Select all.
choices: It's far faster — memory instead of disk
It takes read load off the database
It's the safest place for the only copy of critical data
It's shared, so every app server sees the same value
exercises.why: An in-memory shared cache gives all app servers low-latency access and can absorb repeated reads that would reach the database. Because cache entries may be evicted or lost, critical data still needs a durable source from which the cache can be rebuilt.

exercises.prompt: A message sitting in a queue waiting to be processed — is that state?
choices: No, it's just a message in transit
Yes — it's in-flight state the system must not lose
Only if the message is large
Only if it's been there over a minute
exercises.why: The queued message represents work the system has accepted but not completed, so losing it changes the outcome. Durable queues retain the message until a consumer acknowledges successful processing; redelivery then requires idempotent handling.

exercises.prompt: What's the first question to ask about any new piece of state?
choices: What programming language will read it?
If we lost it, what breaks — and who else needs to read it?
How many bytes is it?
Is it JSON or binary?
exercises.why: The consequence of loss determines durability requirements, and the set of readers determines whether storage must be shared. Those constraints eliminate unsuitable placements before language, encoding, or implementation details matter.

exercises.title: A source of truth is authoritative; derived copies require synchronization
exercises.body: The source of truth is the system whose accepted value resolves disagreement. Caches, replicas, and search indexes hold derived copies for faster or specialized reads. When the authoritative value changes, an update, invalidation, or refresh process must bring each derived copy forward.
exercises.note: A lost invalidation or delayed update serves stale data until another refresh path runs. Time-to-live limits the stale window but does not prevent it.

exercises.prompt: Show the minimum components and flows that implement this mechanism: A source of truth is authoritative; derived copies require synchronization
exercises.why: The source of truth is the system whose accepted value resolves disagreement. Caches, replicas, and search indexes hold derived copies for faster or specialized reads. When the authoritative value changes, an update, invalidation, or refresh process must bring each derived copy forward. A lost invalidation or delayed update serves stale data until another refresh path runs. Time-to-live limits the stale window but does not prevent it.

exercises.prompt: The moment you cache a value so it exists in two places, what problem have you created?
choices: None — you just made it faster
The two copies can disagree — you now own a consistency problem
Only extra storage cost
Only extra latency
exercises.why: After a value exists in the source and a cache, a write can update one copy before the other. The system therefore needs a freshness policy—such as expiration, invalidation, or versioning—and behavior for reads during disagreement.

exercises.prompt: Build the price-update path. A write must reach the authority first; two derived copies are then refreshed or invalidated from that accepted value.
exercises.why: The product database accepts the authoritative price, then refresh or invalidation paths bring the cache and search index forward from that value. If either propagation path is delayed or lost, reads through that derived copy can still serve an older price until retry, repair, or expiry runs.

exercises.prompt: Match each kind of copy to what it is.

pairs.right: The authoritative system or history that resolves disagreement
A fast copy that may be stale
A copy kept in sync, for reads or failover
A copy that no longer matches the truth

exercises.why: The source of truth is authoritative, a cache is a fast copy that may age, a replica is synchronized for read capacity or recovery, and a stale copy no longer reflects the authoritative value. Naming each role makes disagreement and recovery policies explicit.

exercises.prompt: There's a famous joke: 'There are only two hard things in Computer Science: cache invalidation and naming things.' Why is cache invalidation genuinely hard?
choices: Deleting keys is computationally expensive
Knowing WHEN a cached copy became wrong requires knowing every possible thing that could have changed it
Caches don't support deletion
It isn't hard — it's just a joke
exercises.why: A cached value becomes invalid when any relevant source data changes, so every write path must either update or evict affected keys. Time-to-live expiration bounds staleness without precise coordination; explicit invalidation can be fresher but fails when a write path omits it.

exercises.prompt: Your entire cache is accidentally wiped. Is that an outage?
choices: Always a catastrophe — the data is gone
It depends: if it held derived state, it rebuilds from the source of truth — painful but recoverable. If it held the only copy, the data is gone
Never a problem — caches don't matter
Only if it was more than 1GB
exercises.why: A derived cache can repopulate from the source of truth, although a cold-cache surge may overload that source during recovery. If the cache held the only copy, no authoritative data remains to rebuild, turning eviction or loss into permanent data loss.

exercises.prompt: You're displaying a user's account balance in a banking app. Slide toward how aggressively you'd cache it.
exercises.leftLabel: Read the source of truth (correct, slower)
exercises.why: An account balance has a high cost of staleness, so reading authoritative or strongly validated data is the safer default. Aggressive caching lowers read latency and source load but creates a window in which the displayed balance can lag committed transactions.

exercises.title: Durability and access scope define the required state store
exercises.body: For each value, specify the tolerated loss window and the readers that need a consistent view. A disposable rate-limit estimate may use local memory; a durable key shared by all service instances needs an external store whose replication and failure behavior meet that contract.
exercises.note: Non-rebuildable state kept only on one instance is lost on restart and may require sticky routing. Request-local data and rebuildable local caches do not prevent replacement.

exercises.prompt: Where should an e-commerce shopping cart live?
choices: Server RAM — it's the fastest option
It depends on the promise: if users expect their cart on their phone AND laptop, it must be in a database tied to their account
Always in a cookie — it saves database load
In the load balancer
exercises.why: A cart promised across phone and laptop must be stored under the user’s account in shared durable storage. Server RAM or a device cookie cannot independently provide cross-device visibility and survival across server replacement.

exercises.prompt: Uploaded photos are saved on one app server's local disk — so only that server can serve them, and they die with it. Where should they live?
exercises.why: Shared object storage makes each photo accessible to every app server and preserves it independently of any server lifecycle. Local disk would bind reads and durability to one machine, causing missing files after load balancing or replacement.

exercises.prompt: Your app servers must be disposable — any one can die at any moment. Which of these violate that? Select all.
choices: Storing uploaded files on local disk
Keeping user sessions in local memory
Writing logs to stdout to be collected elsewhere
Caching a computed value in local memory that can be recomputed
exercises.why: Uploaded files and sessions in local storage are unique required state, so an instance failure loses data or breaks active users. Externally collected logs already leave the instance, and a reconstructable local cache can be discarded safely.

exercises.prompt: To make `POST /payments` safely retryable, the server stores each idempotency key and its result. What have you just created?
choices: Nothing — it's just a lookup
New state: the server must now durably remember keys, share them across servers, and eventually expire them
A cache, which needs no thought
A queue
exercises.why: The idempotency record is new state that maps an operation key to its completed or in-progress outcome. It must be shared across payment servers, durable across ambiguous failures, and expired only after the retry window closes.

exercises.prompt: You're rate-limiting a paid API where exceeding the limit costs you real money. Slide toward where the counter should live.
exercises.rightLabel: Shared store (exact, adds a network hop)
exercises.why: A local counter enforces a limit only against traffic seen by one server, so requests distributed across servers can exceed the paid global allowance. A shared counter adds a network dependency but coordinates one authoritative total across the fleet.

exercises.prompt: Which state placement is still SERVING you while an entire datacenter sits dark?
choices: Redis running in that datacenter
A database on disk in that datacenter
Data replicated to a database in another region
Server RAM
exercises.why: Only the database replica in another region remains reachable when the entire local datacenter is dark. Local disk may preserve bytes for later recovery, but it cannot provide service while power and networking at that site are unavailable.

exercises.prompt: A teammate says: 'let's just keep it in memory for now — it's faster.' What single question should decide it?
choices: Is memory cheap enough?
'If this server died right now, what would we lose — and who else needs to read this?'
How large is the object?
Which library are we using?
exercises.why: The loss consequence determines whether volatile local memory is acceptable, and the reader set determines whether one server can own the value. Rebuildable instance-private data fits memory; durable or cross-server data requires an appropriate shared store.

exercises.prompt: A shopping cart exists only in one API server's memory. A load balancer sends the next request to another server. What breaks?
choices: The second server cannot reconstruct the cart
DNS resolution becomes slower
HTTP changes from TCP to UDP
The database gains an index
exercises.why: The cart is retained request-to-request state, but only one interchangeable instance owns it. Externalizing or consistently routing that state is required before arbitrary servers can handle later requests.
